Iraq War. From two thousand three to two thousand eleven, an invasion and occupation of Iraq by a United States-led military coalition occurred, justified by claims that Saddam Hussein possessed weapons of mass destruction and posed a threat to global security. The war killed hundreds of thousands, destabilized the region, cost trillions in American resources, and became a defining tragedy of the early twenty-first century.

President George W. Bush authorized the invasion following the September eleventh attacks, linking Hussein to terrorism, a connection later proven baseless. He claimed Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction that were never found. The initial invasion in March two thousand three was swift and militarily successful. American forces defeated Hussein's army in weeks, but the occupation and insurgency that followed would consume far more resources and lives.

The war's rationale was disputed even before invasion. Major allies including France, Germany, and Canada refused to participate. No WMDs were ever discovered. Investigations later concluded the intelligence was distorted or fabricated to justify the war.

The occupation spawned a vicious insurgency fueled by sectarian tensions between Sunni and Shia, American counterinsurgency tactics including Abu Ghraib prison abuse and civilian casualties, and the power vacuum created by disbanding Hussein's military. The Islamic State of Iraq and Syria emerged from the remnants of Hussein's Ba'athist military and the chaos of occupation, eventually seizing large parts of Iraq and neighboring Syria in two thousand fourteen.

American combat troops withdrew in two thousand eleven under President Barack Obama, but the United States maintained military advisors and bases. The war fundamentally altered American credibility internationally and divided the American electorate.

Estimates of Iraqi deaths range from one hundred fifty thousand to six hundred thousand directly from violence or war-related causes. Millions became refugees. American casualties exceeded four thousand four hundred killed and thirty thousand wounded. The invasion and subsequent occupation represent one of the most consequential foreign policy decisions in modern American history.
